name: Colorado

events.title: Statehood
events.text: Colorado became the 38th state on August 1, 1876. Congress gave it 1 seat in the House until the next apportionment.

events.title: 1880 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1880 census, Colorado kept 1 seat in the House. It elected its one member statewide (at-large).

events.title: 1890 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1890 census, Colorado's House delegation grew from 1 to 2 seats.

events.title: 1900 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1900 census, Colorado's House delegation grew from 2 to 3 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 58th through 62nd Congresses (1903–1913), Colorado elected one of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1910 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1910 census, Colorado's House delegation grew from 3 to 4 seats.

events.title: Some members elected at-large
events.text: In the 63rd Congress (1913–1915), Colorado elected 2 of its representatives statewide (at-large) and the rest by district.

events.title: 1930 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1930 census, Colorado kept 4 seats in the House.

events.title: 1940 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1940 census, Colorado kept 4 seats in the House.

events.title: 1950 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1950 census, Colorado kept 4 seats in the House.

events.title: 1960 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1960 census, Colorado kept 4 seats in the House.

events.title: 1970 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1970 census, Colorado's House delegation grew from 4 to 5 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1980 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1980 census, Colorado's House delegation grew from 5 to 6 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1990 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1990 census, Colorado kept 6 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2000 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2000 census, Colorado's House delegation grew from 6 to 7 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Mid-decade redraw struck down
events.text: The legislature passed a new congressional map in 2003, replacing a court-drawn map from 2002. The Colorado Supreme Court ruled in Salazar v. Davidson that the state constitution allows congressional redistricting only once after each census, so the 2002 map stayed in use.

events.title: 2010 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2010 census, Colorado kept 7 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Independent commission created
events.text: Colorado voters approved Amendment Y, creating an independent commission to draw congressional districts. Its first map was used from the 2022 election.

events.title: 2020 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2020 census, Colorado's House delegation grew from 7 to 8 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

compactnessNote: Polsby-Popper compactness (4π × area ÷ perimeter²) measured on the projected district shapes. It describes shape only: coastlines, rivers and county lines lower it too, so a low score is not evidence of intent. "Irregular" marks the least compact 5% of district shapes in each census era nationally.

c053.text: New map drawn after the 1890 census, which raised Colorado's seats from 1 to 2. It was first used in the 1892 election.

c064.text: New map drawn after the 1910 census, which raised Colorado's seats from 3 to 4. It was first used in the 1914 election.

c068.text: Colorado's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1922 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c089.text: New map drawn after the 1960 census, which left Colorado with 4 seats. It was first used in the 1964 election.

c093.text: New map drawn after the 1970 census, which raised Colorado's seats from 4 to 5. It was first used in the 1972 election.

c098.text: New map drawn after the 1980 census, which raised Colorado's seats from 5 to 6. It was first used in the 1982 election.

c103.text: New map drawn after the 1990 census, which left Colorado with 6 seats. It was first used in the 1992 election.

c108.text: New map drawn after the 2000 census, which raised Colorado's seats from 6 to 7. It was first used in the 2002 election.

c113.text: New map drawn after the 2010 census, which left Colorado with 7 seats. It was first used in the 2012 election.

c115.text: Not a new map: the historical boundary records show only slight differences in 3 districts from the previous Congress, and no statewide redistricting is recorded for this election.

c118.text: New map drawn after the 2020 census, which raised Colorado's seats from 7 to 8. It was first used in the 2022 election.
